name: Mandibular advancement device
lead: A mandibular advancement device (MAD), also called a mandibular advancement splint or sleep apnea oral appliance, is a custom-made mouthpiece worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward. It is prescribed mainly for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and some versions are also used for jaw-joint complaints [1].

The appearance link people describe runs through sleep. By keeping the airway open, the device is intended to quiet snoring and reduce breathing interruptions, so the wearer sleeps more continuously. Looksmaxxing writers who discuss sleep generally describe rested skin, less puffiness and brighter eyes as downstream benefits of good sleep, and a MAD sits at the start of that chain for people whose sleep is disrupted by airway collapse [3][6].

Clinically, CPAP is the standard first-line treatment for OSA. The 2015 guideline from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine recommends that sleep physicians consider an oral appliance for adults who cannot tolerate CPAP or who prefer another option, and professional sleep societies likewise recommend oral appliances for primary snoring [15][1][6]. Randomised trials have compared MADs with CPAP on blood pressure and other outcomes [4][7], and systematic reviews have examined how device design affects results [5]. No study has measured facial appearance as an outcome of MAD use.

paras: The appliance fits over the upper and lower teeth and positions the lower jaw forward. Wikipedia lists alternative names including mandibular advancement device, oral airway dilator and sleep apnea mouth guard, and describes the therapy as noninvasive, easily reversible and quiet [1].

Designs vary: some are one-piece monoblock units, others have two parts joined by hinges, struts or straps that allow some jaw movement. Design work has focused on reducing bulk, allowing yawning, talking and drinking, and allowing mouth breathing, which early gum-shield-style devices prevented [1]. Prescription custom-made devices are distinguished from over-the-counter thermoplastic 'boil-and-bite' products; a 2008 comparison cited by Wikipedia concluded the thermoplastic device could not be recommended as a therapeutic option or as a screening tool [1].

Wikipedia also describes newer 3D-printed mouthpieces made from a scan of the patient's mouth, with separate airway channels intended to bypass obstruction from the nose, mouth and tongue, and notes that lower-cost non-prescription devices exist but are regarded by some sleep specialists as unproven and potentially hazardous [1].

Moving the lower jaw forward tightens the soft tissue and muscles of the upper airway and enlarges the space behind the tongue, which reduces collapse during sleep. The tightening also reduces vibration of airway tissue, the most common cause of snoring [1].

Reviews of obstructive sleep apnea describe a narrow, collapsible oropharynx as central to the condition, alongside factors such as muscle tone during sleep stages and arousal threshold [2]. Research on polysomnographic 'endotypes' has examined whether these physiological traits predict who responds to a MAD [11]. A 2008 study cited by Wikipedia found that higher nasal resistance may worsen outcomes with a splint, suggesting a role for combined ENT and sleep-medicine assessment [1].

The 2015 clinical practice guideline on oral appliance therapy, issued jointly by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American Academy of Dental Sleep Medicine, states that sleep physicians should consider an oral appliance rather than no treatment for adults with OSA who cannot tolerate CPAP or who prefer an alternative. It describes CPAP as generally first-line and as superior to oral appliances for reducing the apnea-hypopnea index, arousal index and oxygen desaturation index [15].

The same guideline suggests that when an appliance is prescribed, a qualified dentist should provide a custom, titratable device rather than a non-custom one, because custom devices produced larger reductions in AHI in the studies it reviewed. It also recommends dentist oversight to screen for dental side effects and bite changes, follow-up sleep testing ordered by the physician, and periodic visits with both the dentist and the sleep physician [15].

Review articles aimed at dentists and physicians describe the broader spectrum of sleep-disordered breathing, from snoring to OSA, central apnea and hypoventilation, and place oral appliances among several options alongside CPAP, positional therapy, weight management and surgery [16][18][3]. A chapter on mandibular advancement splint therapy in a medical-biology series covers indications and outcomes in more detail [17].

Reviews state that MADs reduce the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) to varying degrees among patients, with effects on daytime sleepiness observed mainly in more severe OSA and some evidence of lower blood pressure [6]. A review in Sleep Medicine Clinics reports that splints are not as efficacious as CPAP at reducing obstructive events, but that adherence and patient preference are greater, and effects on general health outcomes, cognition and quality of life appear equivalent [4].

Wikipedia reports that MADs tend to be more successful in mild and moderate apnea than severe, that they may lower apnea substantially without eliminating it, and that a meta-analysis of blood-pressure trials found them comparable to CPAP; a 2024 meta-analysis cited there estimated a 66% AHI reduction in severe OSA [1]. Interindividual variability in response is described as the main barrier to routine use, which is why prediction tools and patient phenotyping have been proposed [4].

In a patient survey summarised by Wikipedia, many people stopped using the device because of discomfort, limited benefit or a switch to CPAP, and frequent side effects included dry mouth, tooth pain, dental discomfort and jaw pain [1]. Long-term use was not associated with temporomandibular disorders but was associated with permanent changes in how the upper and lower teeth meet, and appliances needed roughly 0.8 repairs or relines per year [1]. A randomised trial has examined effects of different OSA treatments on the temporomandibular joint [9].

Adherence is linked to patients' concerns about tooth effects, perceived efficacy and comfort [1]. CPAP manufacturers have claimed that poorly fitted devices can shift teeth, a claim Wikipedia notes is made without cited evidence [1].

The AASM and AADSM guideline lists dental side effects and bite (occlusal) changes as the most common category of adverse effect, along with device breakage, allergic reactions to materials such as acrylics or metals, and discomfort. It also notes that people who grind their teeth heavily or have certain anatomical differences may have difficulty, and that discontinuation because of side effects is less common with oral appliances than with CPAP [15]. This is why the guideline calls for ongoing dental follow-up [15].

Community material specific to MADs as an appearance tool is limited. Sleep is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a foundation for skin, eye-area and facial-puffiness appearance, and an airway device fits into that discussion only for people who have snoring or sleep apnea. Because a MAD moves the jaw during sleep rather than reshaping bone, it is distinct from jaw-surgery procedures sometimes discussed under similar names; maxillomandibular advancement is a separate surgical operation reported in the clinical literature [14].

Wikipedia reports that MADs are widely used in the United States and increasingly in the UK, and that in the US most health insurance plans cover part of the cost of a prescription device, with out-of-pocket costs up to about $1,900 [1]. Dentists trained in dental sleep medicine typically fit them, and dental journals have published overviews of sleep-disordered breathing for practitioners [5].

A randomised, noninferiority trial in JACC compared MAD with CPAP for 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure in OSA patients who declined or could not tolerate CPAP [7]. A substudy of a randomised trial in 144 participants with severe OSA compared MAD with CPAP on blood pressure, sleep-related quality of life, myocardial remodelling, heart rhythm and biomarkers [8].

A JAMA Otolaryngology trial compared mandibular advancement with combined airway and positional therapy for snoring [12]. A systematic review of 20 randomised trials and six cohort studies compared MAD designs, finding statistically significant but clinically limited differences in AHI between some designs [5]. Reviews summarise effects on AHI, sleepiness and blood pressure [6]. No studies found on facial-appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A jaw-forward sleep splint for snoring and apnea: a medical device with no appearance evidence.
card.note: Medical sleep device; can permanently change the bite.

quick.overview:
A mandibular advancement device is a custom mouthpiece worn at night that pushes the lower jaw forward to keep the airway open.
Its evidence is for sleep apnea and snoring. No studies have examined it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Holding the lower jaw forward widens the airway behind the tongue during sleep.
quick.risks: Dry mouth, tooth and jaw soreness and lasting changes in how the teeth meet are reported; it is a prescription device.

chain: Holds the lower jaw forward during sleep
Keeps the airway open and reduces snoring and apnea events
Rested look: skin, eyes and facial puffiness
angle.text: A MAD is worn at night to keep the airway open in people with snoring or sleep apnea. Better, less interrupted sleep is the route by which people expect a more rested look; the device itself changes no facial feature.
